I have substantial material from Enduring Word, Gill, Ellicott, and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, with supporting snippets from Keil & Delitzsch, Spurgeon, Maclaren, Henry, and others. However, search and fetch limits prevented me from reaching modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org), Catholic/Orthodox sites, Methodist/Wesleyan sites, and directly reading the Lutheran, Reformed, and Baptist pages beyond what appeared in general search results. Below is what the sources actually say, verse by verse.

---

## 1. VERSE-BY-VERSE TRADITIONAL READING

**Title and Character of the Psalm**

Psalm 130 is the sixth of the seven penitential psalms (Pss 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, 143). Luther famously called these the *Psalmi Paulini* — "the Pauline Psalms" — because "they teach us that the forgiveness of sins is vouchsafed to them that believe without the law and without works." He said Psalm 130 in particular showed him "the gate of heaven opening wide." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gtb/psalms-130.html] It is titled "A Song of Ascents," one of the pilgrim songs (Pss 120–134). Keil & Delitzsch note that the psalm moves through "step-like parallelism," rising from the abyss to the heights of hope. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 1 — "Out of the depths I cry to You, O LORD!"**

The "depths" (Hebrew *maʿamakim*) are a recurrent biblical image for overwhelming distress — deep waters threatening to drown (Ps 69:2, 69:14; Jonah 2:2). The psalmist cries to Yahweh, the covenant God of Israel. David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that while people experience depths of poverty, sorrow, confusion, and pain, the specific depth here is "the depth of the awareness and guilt of sin" (made explicit in v. 3). Spurgeon is quoted: "Pearls lie deep," and "perhaps the sweet singer would never have found that precious thing had he not been cast into the depths."

Gill notes the "depths" could mean a deep sense of sin, or depths of affliction. He adds that Theodoret understood it as crying from the bottom of the heart — sincerity of soul, as opposed to feigned prayer. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown identify the occasion as the low state of the Jews after the return from Babylon, and see Israel corporately crying from deep distress. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

Ellicott: "A recurrent image for overwhelming distress … used literally in Isaiah 51:10 for the sea." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

**v. 2 — "O Lord, hear my voice; let Your ears be attentive to my plea for mercy."**

The psalmist shifts from *Yahweh* (v. 1) to *Adonai* (v. 2) — "Master" or "Ruler." Guzik cites Fausset: "As Jehovah marks God's unchangeable faithfulness to His promises … so Adonai marks His Lordship over all hindrances." The repetition is poetic emphasis. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "It is better for our prayer to be heard than answered. If the Lord were to make an absolute promise to answer all our requests, it might be rather a curse than a blessing." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Gill: "God is a God hearing prayer; sometimes his people think he does not hear them; but he always does, and in his own time answers." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

JFB: "Let thine ears be attentive … Hebrew, Adonai. As Yahweh marks His unchangeable faithfulness … so Adonai His Lordship over all hindrances in the way of His delivering them." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 3 — "If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand?"**

The word "mark" (BSB: "kept track of") is Hebrew *shamar* — "keep, watch, preserve." If God kept a strict account of sins, retaining them in remembrance to punish, no one could stand. JFB: "'Stand' is a legal term for, be justified (cf. Ps 143:2)." To "fall" is to be condemned. JFB also notes the divine name *Jah* (a shortened form of Yahweh) is used here — "the concentrated essence of all that Yahweh implies." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

Ellicott: "If 'Jah' were to watch for men's lapses, as one watches for the dawn, nothing but signal punishment could follow." He commends the observation that "misfortune provokes at this crisis … not murmurings against the Divine dealings, but a sense of deep contrition." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Gill: "Should he keep a watchful eye over them, make strict inspection into them, enter into a critical examination of them … should he visit for them in a way of wrath … all a man's righteousness, repentance, humiliation and tears, would stand him in no stead." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

Guzik quotes Poole: "'To stand' is a judicial phrase, and notes a man's being absolved or justified, upon an equal trial, as Psalm 1:5, Romans 14:4, where it is opposed to falling." Also Clarke: "If thou shouldst set down every deviation in thought, word, and deed from thy holy law … O Lord, who could stand?" [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

The Expositor's Bible (Maclaren) notes the hypothetical form "holds a negation concealed in it" — the thought that God does *not* mark sin in this way is implied, setting up the "for" of v. 4. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 4 — "But with You there is forgiveness, so that You may be feared."**

Several commentators note the Hebrew particle *ki* is better rendered "for" than "but," completing the thought: "Thou wilt not mark iniquities, *for* with Thee there is forgiveness." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

Maclaren: the word for "forgiveness" (Hebrew *selichah*, a late form found only here and in Neh 9:17 and Dan 9:9) "literally means cutting off, and so suggests the merciful surgery by which the cancerous tumour is taken out of the soul." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-130.html]

The phrase "that You may be feared" has been much discussed. The traditional reading is that God's forgiveness produces reverent awe and loving fear in the forgiven — not servile terror but a fear of offending such gracious goodness. JFB: "The sense of God's forgiveness leads His children lovingly to reverence Him, and to shrink with fear from all that would offend Him (1 Kings 8:39-40)." Guzik quotes Swinnock (via Spurgeon): "The hammer of the law may break the icy heart of man with terrors and horrors, and yet it may remain ice still … but when the fire of love kindly thaweth its ice, it is changed and dissolved into water." Guzik also quotes the Welsh revivalist of 1905 who rendered it: "There is forgiveness with Thee — enough to frighten us!" — which G. Campbell Morgan called "fine exposition" if not accurate translation. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Ellicott offers an alternative possibility: "that the manifestation of Divine mercy to Israel may strike fear in the heathen." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Gill sees here a reference to Christ's propitiation: the Septuagint and Vulgate render it "propitiation." "God had found out Christ to be the propitiatory sacrifice for sin … and he is become so; and has made reconciliation for sin." Without forgiveness there would be no godly fear among men — "there might be dread and trembling, as among devils, but no godly fear." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 5 — "I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope."**

Ellicott: "The Hebrew expresses, I have been waiting, and still wait. Mark the earnestness in the repetition, I wait, my soul waits." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Guzik: "The waiting was not passive or inactive. The psalmist used the time to actively set his hope upon God's promises, revealed in His word." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

JFB: "We must not only hope, but wait patiently the Lord's time of realizing our hope. On the other hand, we must not only wait, but blend believing hope with our waiting — not wait in apathy, much less wait as those tired of hoping and so ceasing to hope (Hab 2:3)." The "word" is God's word of promise (Pss 119:74, 81-82, 114, 147). [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

Gill: the "word" refers both to the essential Word (the Messiah, the Hope of Israel) and to the word of promise concerning the coming of Christ, pardon of sin, and eternal life. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

Keil & Delitzsch: "He waits upon God's word, the word of His salvation (Ps 119:81), which, if it penetrates into the soul and cleaves there, calms all unrest." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 6 — "My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning — more than watchmen wait for the morning."**

The doubled line creates an impression of prolonged, intense waiting. The watchmen may be military sentinels longing for relief at daybreak, or Levitical priests watching for the first ray of dawn to begin morning sacrifices (Ellicott cites Ps 134:1 and the Mishnah). The key point: the watchman does *not doubt* that morning will come — he only waits for *when*. So the psalmist waits with certainty, not uncertainty. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Guzik: "The watchman doesn't doubt that morning will come, but only wonders when, and watches for it diligently." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Gill notes several interpretations: city watchmen on the last watch longing for dawn; those sitting up with the sick; priests and Levites watching in the temple to begin morning sacrifices. The Targum renders it: "more than they that observe the morning watches, which they observe to offer up the morning sacrifice." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

Matthew Henry: "Like those who wish to see the dawn, being very desirous that light would come long before day; but still more earnestly does a good man long for the tokens of God's favour, and the visits of his grace." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/psalms-130.html]

Keil & Delitzsch: "The wrath, in the sphere of which the poet now finds himself, is a nightly darkness, out of which he wishes to be removed into the sunny realm of love (Mal 4:2)." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 7 — "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD, for with the LORD is loving devotion, and with Him is redemption in abundance."**

The psalm turns from personal testimony to public exhortation. Ellicott: "Rather (as in Prayer-Book), *Hope Israel in Jehovah*. It is the watchword of faith addressed to the nation." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Maclaren: "In the depths he was alone, and felt as if the only beings in the universe were God and himself. The consciousness of sin isolates, and the sense of forgiveness unites. Whoever has known that 'with Jehovah is pardon' is impelled thereby to invite others." The Hebrew word for "abundant" (or "plenteous") redemption is literally "multiplied." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-130.html]

Spurgeon is quoted by Guzik: "Cease looking for the water, and look for the well. You will more readily see the Savior than see salvation … You will more easily fix your eye on Jesus than upon justification, sanctification, or any other separate blessing." Guzik adds: "The psalmist put his faith and hope in the Lord Himself, not in the mercy or redemption God would bring. He looked to the Giver before the gift." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Gill: the "mercy" (or "loving devotion," Hebrew *chesed*) is "natural and essential" to God; "there is 'grace' with him; an abundance of it in his heart; a fulness of it in his son." Redemption is "plenteous" considering the number of persons redeemed, the completeness of what is redeemed, what they are redeemed *from*, the price paid, and the display of divine attributes. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

---

**v. 8 — "And He will redeem Israel from all iniquity."**

The psalm's confident conclusion. Ellicott: "He — Emphatic. He and only He." And critically: "The redemption must not be limited to the consequences of iniquity, though including these. The psalm belongs to the age of true national contrition, when nothing would satisfy but deliverance from sin, as well as from its punishment." He contrasts Ps 25:22 where the expression is "from all his troubles" — here it is "from all his iniquities." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/psalms-130.html]

Maclaren: "He will redeem Israel from all his iniquities; not only from their consequences in punishment, but from their power, as well as from their guilt and their penalty. The psalmist means something a great deal deeper than deliverance from calamities … He speaks New Testament language." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-130.html]

Gill: Redemption was future when the words were written but certain by God's promise — "of the whole Israel, or elect of God; and that from 'all' their iniquities, original and actual; sins, secret and open, of heart, lip, and life." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

Guzik: "What God has demonstrated in the private life, He will also perform for the community that cries out to Him." And quoting Kidner: "Nothing could be further from the shut-in gloom and uncertainty of 'the depths' than this. The singer is now liberated from himself to turn to his people and to hold out hopes that are far from tentative." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Keil & Delitzsch: "He means complete and final redemption, above all, in the genuinely New Testament manner, spiritual redemption." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-130.html]

## 2. WHERE PROTESTANT TRADITIONS DIFFER

### Lutheran

Luther had a uniquely intense relationship with this psalm. Hastings records that "this was one of the favourite psalms of Luther — one he paraphrased and had set to music; in it, he said he saw the gate of heaven opening wide to him." During the Augsburg Diet at Coburg Castle, when he suffered inward and outward trials and fell into a swoon, on waking he said: "Come and let us, in defiance of the devil, sing the Psalm, 'Lord, from the depths to thee I cry.'" Luther called Pss 32, 51, 130, and 143 the *Psalmi Paulini* because "they teach us that the forgiveness of sins is vouchsafed to them that believe without the law and without works." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gtb/psalms-130.html]

Luther's hymn paraphrase (1524) captures the distinctively Lutheran emphasis on *sola gratia*. Stanza 2: "But love and grace with thee prevail, O God, our sins forgiving; The holiest deeds can naught avail Of all before thee living. Before thee none can boast him clear; Therefore must each thy judgment fear, And live on thy compassion." Stanza 3: "For this, my hope in God shall rest, Naught building on my merit." [https://www.biblehub.com/library/bacon/the_hymns_of_martin_luther/iv_aus_tiefer_noth_schrei.htm]

Hastings records Luther saying that the words "'That thou mayest be feared' thrust away all self-merit, teach us to take off our hat before God and confess, *gratia est, non meritum, remissio non satisfactio* — 'it is all forgiveness, and no merit.'" [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gtb/psalms-130.html]

### Reformed

The Reformed reading emphasises that the ground of forgiveness is entirely in God's character, not human merit, and that forgiveness produces grateful, filial fear rather than servile terror. JFB: "The sense of God's forgiveness leads His children lovingly to reverence Him, and to shrink with fear from all that would offend Him … A harsh God (such as the devil pictures God to the unregenerate) would either be shunned altogether, or be worshipped only in order that He might not hurt us (as the pagan worship their gods)." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-130.html]

Keil & Delitzsch emphasise that "the condemnability of the natural man, the freeness of mercy, and the spiritual nature of redemption are expressed in a manner thoroughly Pauline." The psalm depicts the way of salvation as through faith alone — "believing waiting is likewise the way to salvation." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/psalms-130.html]

The Monergism site (from search excerpt) describes the Winslow exposition as teaching: "your hope does not rest in the strength of your faith, but in the sufficiency of your Savior." [https://www.monergism.com/soul-heights-and-soul-depths-exposition-psalm-130-ebook]

### Baptist (especially Spurgeon)

Spurgeon's emphasis falls on Christ-centered hope and the danger of looking to the gift rather than the Giver. In his sermon "Israel's Hope; or, the Centre of the Target," he writes: "The sinner is not to hasten with his first thoughts to the mercy that he wants, nor even to the promise of God to which he may look; but he is to go to the Lord Jesus Christ himself, as the Lord of mercy, and fountain of redemption. The first exercise of our faith is to deal immediately with the Lord God as he meets us in the person of our Lord Jesus Christ." [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israels-hope-or-the-centre-of-the-target]

Spurgeon sees the psalmist's argument as: "He delivered me. What am I more than others? The gracious Lord who saved me will save all those who call upon him in truth." He also stresses going "straight to God" — "To join another ground of confidence with the Lord is a sort of practical idolatry which is to the wounding of faith." [https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/israels-hope-or-the-centre-of-the-target]

Gill, a Baptist, reads the psalm Christologically throughout: the "propitiation" in v. 4 is specifically Christ's sacrifice; the "word" in v. 5 includes Christ as the essential Word; and v. 8's redemption is "by Christ … complete, and now obtained, and is an eternal one." [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-130.html]

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word)

David Guzik's commentary emphasises personal experience and the move from private despair to public testimony. He stresses that "God's forgiveness is not earned but freely given" and "should awaken in us a reverent fear that keeps us from wanting to sin against such great goodness." The application is experiential: "When we find ourselves in the depths of guilt and shame, we can cry out with confidence that forgiveness truly exists with God." The psalm is read as a pattern: cry from the depths → receive forgiveness → wait patiently → encourage others. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

### Wesleyan/Methodist

James Montgomery Boice, cited by Guzik, records that on the afternoon John Wesley's heart "was strangely warmed" and he truly trusted Christ for salvation, he attended a vesper service at St Paul's Cathedral where Psalm 130 was sung as an anthem. "Wesley was greatly moved by the anthem, and it became one of the means God used to open his heart to the gospel of salvation." [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-130/]

Note: I was unable to search seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu directly due to limits. However, the known Wesleyan emphasis on the "second change" or "entire sanctification" sometimes reads v. 8 ("redeem Israel from *all* iniquity") as pointing toward full deliverance from the power as well as the guilt of sin — a reading Maclaren also articulates, though he is not specifically Wesleyan. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/psalms-130.html]

## 3. OTHER VIEWS

### Catholic Reading

Psalm 130 is known in Catholic tradition as the *De Profundis* (from the Latin Vulgate's opening words) and is one of the seven Penitential Psalms. It is traditionally prayed in the Office of the Dead and as part of the evening prayer of the Church. The Vulgate reads v. 4 as "propitiation" rather than "forgiveness," connecting the psalm to Christ's atoning sacrifice.

### Orthodox Reading

I was unable to search oca.org within the available limits. In Orthodox tradition, Psalm 130 is read regularly in the services, especially during Lent, as one of the penitential psalms.

### Modern Scholarship

I was unable to search bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org due to search limits. However, Ellicott and Keil & Delitzsch already incorporate critical philological notes (the Hebrew *ki* as "for," the late form *selichah*, the "step-like parallelism") that represent the best of 19th-century scholarship. Maclaren also notes the form-critical observation that vv. 7-8 are "evidently taken up by the full choir," suggesting liturgical use.

### Lutheran Hymn Tradition (historical note)

Luther's hymn *Aus tiefer Noth schrei' ich zu dir* (1524) became one of the foundational chorales of the Lutheran Reformation. Stanza 5: "What though our sins are manifold? Supreme his mercy reigneth; No limit can his hand withhold, Where evil most obtaineth. He the good Shepherd is alone, Who Israel will redeem and won, Forgiving all transgression." [https://www.biblehub.com/library/bacon/the_hymns_of_martin_luther/iv_aus_tiefer_noth_schrei.htm]

---

**Summary of the Psalm's Movement (across all traditions)**

The psalm climbs four stages: (1) a desperate cry from the depths of sin (vv. 1-2); (2) the foundation of hope — God's forgiving character (vv. 3-4); (3) patient, word-anchored waiting (vv. 5-6); (4) public exhortation and confident assurance of full redemption for all God's people (vv. 7-8). Across all the traditions consulted, there is remarkable agreement on the core meaning: salvation is by grace alone, forgiveness is in God's nature, and the proper response is reverent fear, patient hope, and evangelistic testimony.
